claim: DCC receptor associates with ribosomes in Xenopus laevis embryonic brains and eyes.
source: We first asked whether the interaction of DCC with ribosomes is conserved in a different system and cell type, and explored the possibility that the Sema3A receptor, Neuropilin-1 (Nrp1), also interacts with ribosomes in this system. To do this, we performed immunoprecipitation (IP) of endogenous DCC and Nrp1 from Xenopus laevis embryonic brains and eyes followed by mass-spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis of eluted samples.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry analysis from Xenopus tissue.

claim: Neuropilin-1 receptor associates with ribosomes in Xenopus laevis embryonic brains and eyes.
source: We first asked whether the interaction of DCC with ribosomes is conserved in a different system and cell type, and explored the possibility that the Sema3A receptor, Neuropilin-1 (Nrp1), also interacts with ribosomes in this system. To do this, we performed immunoprecipitation (IP) of endogenous DCC and Nrp1 from Xenopus laevis embryonic brains and eyes followed by mass-spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis of eluted samples.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry analysis from Xenopus tissue.

claim: 'Structural constituent of ribosomes' is the most prominently enriched category in both DCC and Nrp1 pulldowns.
source: Gene-ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that 'structural constituent of ribosomes' appeared as the most prominently enriched category in both DCC and Nrp1 pulldowns, indicating that both receptors can interact with ribosomal proteins (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 75 out of 79 ribosomal proteins (94.9%) were detected in the DCC and Nrp1 pulldowns.
source: Specifically, 75 out of 79 ribosomal proteins (94.9%) were detected in the DCC and Nrp1 pulldowns.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: 51 ribosomal proteins were identified as statistically enriched interactors for Nrp1 compared to IgG control pulldowns.
source: Of these, 51 and 33 RPs were identified as statistically enriched interactors for Nrp1 and DCC, respectively, compared to IgG control pulldowns.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: 33 ribosomal proteins were identified as statistically enriched interactors for DCC compared to IgG control pulldowns.
source: Of these, 51 and 33 RPs were identified as statistically enriched interactors for Nrp1 and DCC, respectively, compared to IgG control pulldowns.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: There was no bias towards small or large ribosomal subunit proteins in DCC and Nrp1 pulldowns.
source: There was no bias towards small or large ribosomal subunit proteins (Figure 1A, red dots).
evidence: Supported by analysis of mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Both DCC and Nrp1 interact with small (40S) and large (60S) ribosomal subunit proteins.
source: To confirm the interaction between receptors and ribosomal proteins, we performed Western blot (WB) analysis after IP and validated that both DCC and Nrp1 interact with small (40S) and large (60S) ribosomal subunit proteins (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis after immunoprecipitation shown in Figures 1C-D.

claim: The interaction between DCC and ribosomal proteins is conserved in human neuronal cell line SH-SY5Y.
source: These interactions appear to be conserved, as endogenous IP from the human neuronal cell line SH-SY5Y, which expresses both DCC and Nrp1, also shows ribosomal protein co-precipitation after pulldown of the endogenous receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation experiments in SH-SY5Y cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The interaction between Nrp1 and ribosomal proteins is conserved in human neuronal cell line SH-SY5Y.
source: These interactions appear to be conserved, as endogenous IP from the human neuronal cell line SH-SY5Y, which expresses both DCC and Nrp1, also shows ribosomal protein co-precipitation after pulldown of the endogenous receptor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation experiments in SH-SY5Y cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Robo2 interacts with ribosomal proteins of both small and large subunits in Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes.
source: Therefore, we asked whether Robo2 also interacts with ribosomal proteins. WB after IP from Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes or SH-SY5Y cells showed that Robo2 also interacts with ribosomal proteins of both subunits (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Robo2 interacts with ribosomal proteins of both small and large subunits in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Therefore, we asked whether Robo2 also interacts with ribosomal proteins. WB after IP from Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes or SH-SY5Y cells showed that Robo2 also interacts with ribosomal proteins of both subunits (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EphB2 does not interact with ribosomal proteins in Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes.
source: In this case, we could not detect co-IP of ribosomal proteins with EphB2 in Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes, indicating that not all guidance receptors interact with ribosomal proteins (Figure 1F), and suggesting that only receptors that require local protein synthesis for their action on growth cones are coupled to ribosomes.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Only receptors that require local protein synthesis for their action on growth cones are coupled to ribosomes.
source: In this case, we could not detect co-IP of ribosomal proteins with EphB2 in Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes, indicating that not all guidance receptors interact with ribosomal proteins (Figure 1F), and suggesting that only receptors that require local protein synthesis for their action on growth cones are coupled to ribosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EphB2, which does not require local protein synthesis, does not interact with ribosomes, while DCC, Nrp1, and Robo2, which do require local protein synthesis, interact with ribosomes.

claim: DCC exhibits significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains.
source: Consistent with the WB results, DCC, Nrp1 and Robo2, but not EphB2, exhibit a significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to an IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains (Figure 1G–J), and in SH-SY5Y cells in the case of DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of rRNA after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Nrp1 exhibits significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains.
source: Consistent with the WB results, DCC, Nrp1 and Robo2, but not EphB2, exhibit a significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to an IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains (Figure 1G–J), and in SH-SY5Y cells in the case of DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of rRNA after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Robo2 exhibits significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains.
source: Consistent with the WB results, DCC, Nrp1 and Robo2, but not EphB2, exhibit a significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to an IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains (Figure 1G–J), and in SH-SY5Y cells in the case of DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of rRNA after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1I.

claim: EphB2 does not exhibit significant enrichment of 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains.
source: Consistent with the WB results, DCC, Nrp1 and Robo2, but not EphB2, exhibit a significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to an IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains (Figure 1G–J), and in SH-SY5Y cells in the case of DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of rRNA after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1J.

claim: DCC exhibits significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to IgG control pulldown in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Consistent with the WB results, DCC, Nrp1 and Robo2, but not EphB2, exhibit a significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to an IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains (Figure 1G–J), and in SH-SY5Y cells in the case of DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of rRNA after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Nrp1 exhibits significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to IgG control pulldown in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Consistent with the WB results, DCC, Nrp1 and Robo2, but not EphB2, exhibit a significant enrichment of both 18S rRNA and 28S rRNA compared to an IgG control pulldown in Xenopus brains (Figure 1G–J), and in SH-SY5Y cells in the case of DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis of rRNA after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Multiple receptors known to trigger local protein synthesis can associate with ribosomal subunits.
source: Collectively, these findings reveal that multiple receptors known to trigger local protein synthesis can associate with ribosomal subunits.
evidence: Supported by the collective data showing DCC, Nrp1, and Robo2 associate with ribosomal subunits.

claim: DCC was prominent in 40S, 60S and 80S fractions but not in polysomal fractions in Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Tcherkezian et al., 2010), DCC was prominent in 40S, 60S and 80S fractions but not in polysomal fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient purification and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nrp1 was found in 40S, 60S and 80S fractions, as well as in polysomal fractions in Xenopus embryonic brains and eyes.
source: Nrp1, however, was found in 40S, 60S and 80S fractions, as well as in polysomal fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a possibly different association mechanism or a different translational status of the receptor-bound ribosomes.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient purification and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both DCC and Nrp1 were present in ribosome-free fractions indicating that not all receptor molecules are associated with ribosomes.
source: Both DCC and Nrp1 were also present in ribosome-free fractions indicating that not all receptor molecules are associated with ribosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient purification and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: EDTA treatment shifted both DCC and Nrp1 to lighter fractions, supporting a valid association with ribosomes.
source: EDTA treatment, which dissociates the monosomes/polysomes into separate ribosomal subunits (Simsek et al., 2017), shifted both DCC and Nrp1 to lighter fractions, supporting a valid association with ribosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient purification with EDTA treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: EDTA treatment before elution significantly decreased the enrichment of 18S and 28S rRNA after DCC pulldown.
source: When IP samples were treated with EDTA before elution, the enrichment of 18S and 28S rRNA after receptor pulldown was significantly decreased for both DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis after EDTA treatment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: EDTA treatment before elution significantly decreased the enrichment of 18S and 28S rRNA after Nrp1 pulldown.
source: When IP samples were treated with EDTA before elution, the enrichment of 18S and 28S rRNA after receptor pulldown was significantly decreased for both DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis after EDTA treatment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RNase A/T1 treatment significantly decreased the co-precipitation of 18S and 28S rRNA with DCC.
source: The significant decrease in the co-precipitation of 18S and 28S rRNA with receptors in these conditions suggests that mRNA is important for the association of 80S ribosomes with receptors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis after RNase A/T1 treatment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: RNase A/T1 treatment significantly decreased the co-precipitation of 18S and 28S rRNA with Nrp1.
source: The significant decrease in the co-precipitation of 18S and 28S rRNA with receptors in these conditions suggests that mRNA is important for the association of 80S ribosomes with receptors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis after RNase A/T1 treatment shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mRNA is important for the association of 80S ribosomes with receptors.
source: The significant decrease in the co-precipitation of 18S and 28S rRNA with receptors in these conditions suggests that mRNA is important for the association of 80S ribosomes with receptors (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RNase A/T1 treatment decreases rRNA co-precipitation with receptors.

claim: Western blot analysis of IP samples treated with RNase A/T1 or EDTA after pulldown confirms the decrease in ribosomal proteins for both DCC and Nrp1.
source: Consistent with these results, Western blot analysis of IP samples treated with RNase A/T1 or EDTA after pulldown confirms the decrease in ribosomal proteins for both DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 2B,C), while the amounts of DCC and Nrp1 that precipitated were unaffected by the treatment conditions (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The amounts of DCC and Nrp1 that precipitated were unaffected by RNase A/T1 or EDTA treatment conditions.
source: Consistent with these results, Western blot analysis of IP samples treated with RNase A/T1 or EDTA after pulldown confirms the decrease in ribosomal proteins for both DCC and Nrp1 (Figure 2B,C), while the amounts of DCC and Nrp1 that precipitated were unaffected by the treatment conditions (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The interaction of receptors with ribosomes is likely mediated through mRNA.
source: Together, these results suggest that the interaction of receptors with ribosomes is likely mediated through mRNA.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing that RNase treatment decreases receptor-ribosome association.

claim: Several RBPs are significantly enriched after DCC or Nrp1 pulldown.
source: Our MS analysis revealed that several RBPs are significantly enriched after DCC or Nrp1 pulldown (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Of 22 RBPs pulled down with DCC and 37 RBPs pulled down with Nrp1, only 11 are shared between the two receptors.
source: Of 22 RBPs pulled down with DCC and 37 RBPs pulled down with Nrp1, only 11 are shared between the two receptors (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Staufen1 is significantly enriched after Nrp1 IP, but not DCC IP.
source: For example, Staufen1 is significantly enriched after Nrp1 IP, but not DCC IP, whereas hnRNPA2B1 is only detected after DCC IP (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: hnRNPA2B1 is only detected after DCC IP.
source: For example, Staufen1 is significantly enriched after Nrp1 IP, but not DCC IP, whereas hnRNPA2B1 is only detected after DCC IP (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: DCC co-localized with hnRNPA2B1 to a higher degree than with Staufen1 in axonal growth cones.
source: DCC co-localized with hnRNPA2B1 to a higher degree than with Staufen1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by dual immunocytochemistry analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nrp1 showed a higher degree of co-localization with Staufen1 compared to hnRNPA2B1 in axonal growth cones.
source: Conversely, Nrp1 showed a higher degree of co-localization with Staufen1 compared to hnRNPA2B1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by dual immunocytochemistry analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The interaction of Staufen1 with Nrp1 was partly decreased by RNAse A/T1 treatment.
source: Western blot quantification after pulldown showed that the interaction of Staufen1 with Nrp1 was partly decreased by RNAse A/T1 treatment, suggesting that mRNA may stabilize the interaction between receptors and RBPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis after RNase treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: mRNA may stabilize the interaction between receptors and RBPs.
source: Western blot quantification after pulldown showed that the interaction of Staufen1 with Nrp1 was partly decreased by RNAse A/T1 treatment, suggesting that mRNA may stabilize the interaction between receptors and RBPs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RNase treatment decreases RBP-receptor interaction.

claim: Receptors associate with specific RBPs, which bind specific mRNAs, and these mRNAs, in turn, recruit ribosomes.
source: Together with our evidence implicating mRNA in the association of receptors with ribosomes, these results are consistent with a model in which receptors associate with specific RBPs, which bind specific mRNAs, and these mRNAs, in turn, recruit ribosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data on receptor-RBP-mRNA-ribosome associations.

claim: DCC and Nrp1 each differentially bind to specific subsets of mRNAs, with 541 mRNAs differentially binding between DCC and Nrp1 (158 mRNAs for DCC versus 383 mRNAs for Nrp1).
source: Differential expression analysis revealed that DCC and Nrp1 each differentially bind to specific subsets of mRNAs, with 541 mRNAs differentially binding between DCC and Nrp1 (158 mRNAs for DCC versus 383 mRNAs for Nrp1) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Of the highly abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM >100), ~41% were differential between DCC and Nrp1.
source: Of the highly abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM >100 and FPKM >1000), ~41% and ~70% respectively were differential between DCC and Nrp1, whilst with the low abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM 1–10), only ~5% were differential between DCC and Nrp1.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Of the highly abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM >1000), ~70% were differential between DCC and Nrp1.
source: Of the highly abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM >100 and FPKM >1000), ~41% and ~70% respectively were differential between DCC and Nrp1, whilst with the low abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM 1–10), only ~5% were differential between DCC and Nrp1.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Of the low abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM 1–10), only ~5% were differential between DCC and Nrp1.
source: Of the highly abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM >100 and FPKM >1000), ~41% and ~70% respectively were differential between DCC and Nrp1, whilst with the low abundant detected mRNAs (FPKM 1–10), only ~5% were differential between DCC and Nrp1.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: GO terms 'cell-cell adhesion' and 'protein targeting' were associated with high abundance mRNAs pulled down with DCC.
source: For the high abundance mRNAs, GO terms that were associated with the mRNAs pulled down with DCC included 'cell-cell adhesion' and 'protein targeting, while 'translation' and 'small GTPase mediated signal transduction' were associated with Nrp1.
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA-sequencing data.

claim: GO terms 'translation' and 'small GTPase mediated signal transduction' were associated with high abundance mRNAs pulled down with Nrp1.
source: For the high abundance mRNAs, GO terms that were associated with the mRNAs pulled down with DCC included 'cell-cell adhesion' and 'protein targeting, while 'translation' and 'small GTPase mediated signal transduction' were associated with Nrp1.
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis of RNA-sequencing data.

claim: There is significant enrichment of known targets of Staufen1 and hnRNPA2B1 in Nrp1 versus DCC pulldown, respectively.
source: The analysis revealed significant enrichment of known targets of Staufen1 and hnRNPA2B1 in Nrp1 versus DCC pulldown, respectively (Mann-Whitney U test, Wilcoxon rank sum test; p=0.001511) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis comparing RNA-seq data with known RBP targets shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The known targets of the 4 RBPs tested (Staufen1, hnRNPA2B1, Elavl1 and Fxr1) can account for 41.1% of the significantly enriched DCC-precipitated RNAs.
source: Overall, the known targets of the 4 RBPs tested (Staufen1, hnRNPA2B1, Elavl1 and Fxr1) can account for 41.1% of the significantly enriched DCC-precipitated RNAs and for 43.1% of the significantly enriched Nrp1-precipitated mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNA-seq data compared with known RBP targets from CLIP studies.

claim: The known targets of the 4 RBPs tested (Staufen1, hnRNPA2B1, Elavl1 and Fxr1) can account for 43.1% of the significantly enriched Nrp1-precipitated mRNAs.
source: Overall, the known targets of the 4 RBPs tested (Staufen1, hnRNPA2B1, Elavl1 and Fxr1) can account for 41.1% of the significantly enriched DCC-precipitated RNAs and for 43.1% of the significantly enriched Nrp1-precipitated mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by analysis of RNA-seq data compared with known RBP targets from CLIP studies.

claim: Receptor-specific RBPs mediate the differential association of mRNAs to receptors.
source: Collectively, the results support a model where receptor-specific RBPs mediate the differential association of mRNAs to receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing receptor-specific RBP and mRNA associations.

claim: DCC and RPL5/uL18 partially co-localized in retinal growth cones and filopodia.
source: DCC and RPL5/uL18 partially co-localized in retinal growth cones and filopodia (Figure 3A, white arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by expansion microscopy imaging shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RPS3A/eS1 co-localized with Nrp1 in retinal growth cones.
source: Similarly, RPS3A/eS1 co-localized with Nrp1 in retinal growth cones (Figure 3B, white arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by expansion microscopy imaging shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Quantification of co-localization in expanded growth cones indicated a positive association between DCC and RPL5/uL18 (Pearson's correlation = 0.4316 ± 0.011, n = 73).
source: Quantification of co-localization in expanded growth cones indicated a positive association between DCC and RPL5/uL18 (Pearson's correlation = 0.4316 ± 0.011, n = 73) and Nrp1 and RPS3A/eS1 (Pearson's correlation = 0.6727 ± 0.014, n = 72) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantification of expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Quantification of co-localization in expanded growth cones indicated a positive association between Nrp1 and RPS3A/eS1 (Pearson's correlation = 0.6727 ± 0.014, n = 72).
source: Quantification of co-localization in expanded growth cones indicated a positive association between DCC and RPL5/uL18 (Pearson's correlation = 0.4316 ± 0.011, n = 73) and Nrp1 and RPS3A/eS1 (Pearson's correlation = 0.6727 ± 0.014, n = 72) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantification of expansion microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Abundant PLA signal was detected between DCC and RPL5/uL18 in retinal axonal growth cones.
source: This control generated a very low amount of background PLA signal (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), while we detected abundant PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18, in line with previous findings (Konopacki et al., 2016), as well as with RPS4X/eS4 or RPL10A/uL1 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Abundant PLA signal was detected between DCC and RPS4X/eS4 in retinal axonal growth cones.
source: This control generated a very low amount of background PLA signal (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), while we detected abundant PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18, in line with previous findings (Konopacki et al., 2016), as well as with RPS4X/eS4 or RPL10A/uL1 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Abundant PLA signal was detected between DCC and RPL10A/uL1 in retinal axonal growth cones.
source: This control generated a very low amount of background PLA signal (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), while we detected abundant PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18, in line with previous findings (Konopacki et al., 2016), as well as with RPS4X/eS4 or RPL10A/uL1 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nrp1 generated abundant PLA signal together with RPS3A/eS1 in retinal axonal growth cones.
source: Similarly, Nrp1 generated abundant PLA signal together with RPS3A/eS1 or RPS23/uS12, with no detectable PLA signal in the negative control (Nrp1-IgG PLA) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Nrp1 generated abundant PLA signal together with RPS23/uS12 in retinal axonal growth cones.
source: Similarly, Nrp1 generated abundant PLA signal together with RPS3A/eS1 or RPS23/uS12, with no detectable PLA signal in the negative control (Nrp1-IgG PLA) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PLA between EphB2 and RPL5/uL18 generated almost no detectable signal compared to DCC-RPL5/uL18 or Nrp1-RPS3A/eS1 in growth cones.
source: Consistent with the IP results (Figure 1F,J) and with the EphB2-induced local protein synthesis independent growth cone collapse (Mann et al., 2003), PLA between EphB2 and RPL5/uL18 generated almost no detectable signal compared to DCC-RPL5/uL18 or Nrp1-RPS3A/eS1 in growth cones (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Ribosomes could be seen aligned in rows underneath the plasma membrane in axonal growth cones.
source: Strikingly, ribosomes could be seen aligned in rows underneath the plasma membrane (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E), particularly in the regions in closest contact with the culture substrate.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy imaging shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Rows of ribosomes within 50 nm of the plasma membrane were observed in 20 out of 22 axonal growth cones.
source: Indeed, we observed rows of ribosomes within 50 nm of the plasma membrane in 20 out of 22 axonal growth cones, and the presence of single 'isolated' ribosomes in the other two growth cones (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The average distance between two neighboring ribosomes close to the plasma membrane in growth cones was significantly larger than the distance between ribosomes in the cell soma (58.12 ± 19.68 nm, n = 93 from 10 growth cones versus 23.05 ± 3.07 nm, n = 158 from five soma, p<0.00001).
source: The average distance between two neighboring ribosomes close to the plasma membrane in growth cones was significantly larger than the distance between ribosomes in the cell soma (58.12 ± 19.68 nm, n = 93 from 10 growth cones versus 23.05 ± 3.07 nm, n = 158 from five soma, p<0.00001) (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,E), indicative of and consistent with monosomes binding to the intracellular portions of transmembrane receptors, such as DCC or Nrp-1.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,E.

claim: The PLA signal between DCC and the ribosomal proteins RPL5/uL18 and RPS4X/eS4 decreased significantly in retinal axon growth cones after 2 min of Netrin-1 stimulation.
source: Remarkably, the PLA signal between DCC and the ribosomal proteins RPL5/uL18 and RPS4X/eS4 decreased significantly in retinal axon growth cones after 2 min of Netrin-1 stimulation (Figure 3H), suggesting a rapid dissociation of ribosomes from the receptor.
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay after Netrin-1 stimulation shown in Figure 3H.

claim: DCC protein level does not change in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation.
source: It should be noted that, whereas DCC protein level does not change in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, both RPL5/uL18 and RPS4X/eS4 are up-regulated in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation (Cagnetta et al., 2018), indicating that the decrease in the PLA signal in response to Netrin-1 may be underestimated.
evidence: Supported by previous proteomics study cited.

claim: Both RPL5/uL18 and RPS4X/eS4 are up-regulated in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation.
source: It should be noted that, whereas DCC protein level does not change in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, both RPL5/uL18 and RPS4X/eS4 are up-regulated in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation (Cagnetta et al., 2018), indicating that the decrease in the PLA signal in response to Netrin-1 may be underestimated.
evidence: Supported by previous proteomics study cited.

claim: The PLA signal between DCC and the RBP hnRNPA2B1 did not decrease after 2 min of Netrin-1 stimulation.
source: In contrast to the DCC-RP PLA signal, the PLA signal between DCC and the RBP hnRNPA2B1 did not decrease after 2 min of Netrin-1 stimulation, indicating that the receptor-RBP interaction is not affected by cue stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay after Netrin-1 stimulation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The receptor-RBP interaction is not affected by cue stimulation.
source: In contrast to the DCC-RP PLA signal, the PLA signal between DCC and the RBP hnRNPA2B1 did not decrease after 2 min of Netrin-1 stimulation, indicating that the receptor-RBP interaction is not affected by cue stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DCC-hnRNPA2B1 PLA signal does not decrease after Netrin-1 stimulation.

claim: Extracellular Sema3A at a concentration of 150 ng/ml triggers a significant decrease in the Nrp1-RPS3A/eS1 and RPS23/uS12 PLA signal within 2 min.
source: Extracellular Sema3A at a concentration of 150 ng/ml, which is known to affect local axonal translation (Manns et al., 2012; Nédelec et al., 2012), also triggers a significant decrease in the Nrp1-RPS3A/eS1 and RPS23/uS12 PLA signal within 2 min (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay after Sema3A stimulation shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Sema3A at 700 ng/ml induces growth cone collapse that is independent of protein synthesis.
source: Interestingly, when Sema3A is presented extracellularly at a higher concentration (700 ng/ml), it induces growth cone collapse that is independent of protein synthesis (Nédelec et al., 2012; Manns et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: Stimulation with 700 ng/ml Sema3A shows no increase in global translation in growth cones.
source: Puromycylation of newly synthesized proteins in axon-only cultures and subsequent visualization and quantification of immunofluorescence using an anti-puromycin antibody (Schmidt et al., 2009) in the presence of 700 ng/ml Sema3A shows no increase in global translation in growth cones (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by puromycylation assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Stimulation with 700 ng/ml Sema3A does not cause a rapid decrease in the Nrp1-RPS3A/eS1 PLA signal.
source: In line with this finding, stimulation with 700 ng/ml Sema3A does not cause a rapid decrease in the Nrp1-RPS3A/eS1 PLA signal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay after high concentration Sema3A stimulation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The dissociation of ribosomes from Nrp1 in response to Sema3A is intimately linked to rapid and local protein synthesis.
source: This suggested that the dissociation of ribosomes from Nrp1 in response to Sema3A is intimately linked to rapid and local protein synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sema3A at concentrations that induce local translation causes ribosome dissociation, while concentrations that do not induce local translation do not cause dissociation.

claim: Nrp1, RPS3A/eS1 and RPS23/uS12 protein levels do not change in response to 5 min Sema3A stimulation.
source: Importantly, the detected decrease in PLA signal is not due to changes in Nrp1, RPS3A/eS1 and RPS23/uS12 protein levels as these do not change in response to 5 min Sema3A stimulation (Cagnetta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by previous proteomics study cited.

claim: Sema3A stimulation does not decrease the PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18.
source: Next, we tested the specificity of the cue-induced dissociation of RPs from receptors by quantifying the PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18 after Sema3A stimulation and the PLA signal between Nrp1 and RPS23/uS12 after Netrin-1 stimulation. In neither case did we observe a decrease in PLA signal, confirming the ligand-receptor specificity of the cue-induced RP dissociation (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay after cross-stimulation shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Netrin-1 stimulation does not decrease the PLA signal between Nrp1 and RPS23/uS12.
source: Next, we tested the specificity of the cue-induced dissociation of RPs from receptors by quantifying the PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18 after Sema3A stimulation and the PLA signal between Nrp1 and RPS23/uS12 after Netrin-1 stimulation. In neither case did we observe a decrease in PLA signal, confirming the ligand-receptor specificity of the cue-induced RP dissociation (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay after cross-stimulation shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The cue-induced RP dissociation is ligand-receptor specific.
source: Next, we tested the specificity of the cue-induced dissociation of RPs from receptors by quantifying the PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18 after Sema3A stimulation and the PLA signal between Nrp1 and RPS23/uS12 after Netrin-1 stimulation. In neither case did we observe a decrease in PLA signal, confirming the ligand-receptor specificity of the cue-induced RP dissociation (Figure 3J–K).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only cognate ligand-receptor pairs show ribosome dissociation.

claim: DCC and Nrp1 receptors are rapidly endocytosed after cue stimulation (1–2 min) in growth cones.
source: Indeed, DCC and Nrp1 receptors are known to be rapidly endocytosed after cue stimulation (1–2 min) in growth cones (Piper et al., 2005) and we have recently identified the presence of ribosomal proteins on axonal endosomes which serve as platforms for local translation (Cioni et al., 2019), raising the possibility that the observed dissociation between receptors and ribosomes may also take place on endosomes.
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are present on axonal endosomes which serve as platforms for local translation.
source: Indeed, DCC and Nrp1 receptors are known to be rapidly endocytosed after cue stimulation (1–2 min) in growth cones (Piper et al., 2005) and we have recently identified the presence of ribosomal proteins on axonal endosomes which serve as platforms for local translation (Cioni et al., 2019), raising the possibility that the observed dissociation between receptors and ribosomes may also take place on endosomes.
evidence: Supported by previous study cited.

claim: Treatment with Dynasore completely blocked the Netrin-1-induced decrease in PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18.
source: Indeed, we found that treatment with the inhibitor of endocytosis Dynasore, a small GTPase inhibitor targeting dynamin (Macia et al., 2006), completely blocked the Netrin-1-induced decrease in PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18, indicating that endocytosis is required for the receptor-ribosome dissociation (Figure 3L).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay with Dynasore treatment shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Endocytosis is required for the receptor-ribosome dissociation.
source: Indeed, we found that treatment with the inhibitor of endocytosis Dynasore, a small GTPase inhibitor targeting dynamin (Macia et al., 2006), completely blocked the Netrin-1-induced decrease in PLA signal between DCC and RPL5/uL18, indicating that endocytosis is required for the receptor-ribosome dissociation (Figure 3L).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking endocytosis prevents receptor-ribosome dissociation.

claim: The rapid cue-specific dissociation of ribosomes in response to extracellular guidance cues is shared among different receptors.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the rapid cue-specific dissociation of ribosomes in response to extracellular guidance cues is shared among different receptors, is tightly linked to cue-induced local translation-dependent responses, and requires endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing multiple receptors exhibit cue-induced ribosome dissociation.

claim: The rapid cue-specific dissociation of ribosomes is tightly linked to cue-induced local translation-dependent responses.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the rapid cue-specific dissociation of ribosomes in response to extracellular guidance cues is shared among different receptors, is tightly linked to cue-induced local translation-dependent responses, and requires endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only cue concentrations that induce local translation cause ribosome dissociation.

claim: The rapid cue-specific dissociation of ribosomes requires endocytosis.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the rapid cue-specific dissociation of ribosomes in response to extracellular guidance cues is shared among different receptors, is tightly linked to cue-induced local translation-dependent responses, and requires endocytosis.
evidence: Supported by the Dynasore experiment showing endocytosis is required.

claim: EphrinA1 has been reported to decrease local translation in hippocampal axons.
source: The cue EphrinA1 has been reported to decrease local translation in hippocampal axons (Nie et al., 2010) and the rapid local translation of the Translationally controlled tumor protein (Tctp), which is up-regulated by Netrin-1 (Gouveia Roque and Holt, 2018).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: EphrinA1 decreases the rapid local translation of Tctp, which is up-regulated by Netrin-1.
source: The cue EphrinA1 has been reported to decrease local translation in hippocampal axons (Nie et al., 2010) and the rapid local translation of the Translationally controlled tumor protein (Tctp), which is up-regulated by Netrin-1 (Gouveia Roque and Holt, 2018).
evidence: Supported by previous study cited.

claim: Netrin-1 induces a decrease in the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal within 2 min.
source: Whereas Netrin-1 induces a decrease in the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal within 2 min, both Ephrin-A1 stimulation alone and co-stimulation with Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 do not decrease the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal, indicating that the Netrin-1-induced dissociation of ribosomes from DCC is blocked by co-stimulation with EphrinA1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: EphrinA1 stimulation alone does not decrease the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal.
source: Whereas Netrin-1 induces a decrease in the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal within 2 min, both Ephrin-A1 stimulation alone and co-stimulation with Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 do not decrease the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal, indicating that the Netrin-1-induced dissociation of ribosomes from DCC is blocked by co-stimulation with EphrinA1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Co-stimulation with Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 does not decrease the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal.
source: Whereas Netrin-1 induces a decrease in the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal within 2 min, both Ephrin-A1 stimulation alone and co-stimulation with Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 do not decrease the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal, indicating that the Netrin-1-induced dissociation of ribosomes from DCC is blocked by co-stimulation with EphrinA1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Netrin-1-induced dissociation of ribosomes from DCC is blocked by co-stimulation with EphrinA1.
source: Whereas Netrin-1 induces a decrease in the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal within 2 min, both Ephrin-A1 stimulation alone and co-stimulation with Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 do not decrease the DCC-RPL5/uL18 PLA signal, indicating that the Netrin-1-induced dissociation of ribosomes from DCC is blocked by co-stimulation with EphrinA1 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that co-stimulation prevents the decrease in PLA signal seen with Netrin-1 alone.

claim: Co-stimulation with EphrinA1 and Sema3A does not block the Sema3A-induced decrease in the Nrp1-RPS23/uS12 PLA signal.
source: By contrast, co-stimulation with EphrinA1 and Sema3A does not block the Sema3A-induced decrease in the Nrp1-RPS23/uS12 PLA signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by proximity ligation assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Integration of guidance cues can alter the receptor-ribosome dissociation.
source: These results reveal that integration of guidance cues can alter the receptor-ribosome dissociation, possibly by structural changes of the interacting receptors (Morales and Kania, 2017; Dudanova and Klein, 2013; Poliak et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EphrinA1 blocks Netrin-1-induced ribosome dissociation from DCC.

claim: Both Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 decrease global local translation in axons.
source: In the culture conditions used in this study (Höpker et al., 1999), both Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 decrease global local translation in axons as measured by the puromycylation assay in axon-only cultures (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Supported by puromycylation assay shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: Both Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 decrease pERK1/2 levels.
source: Consistent with this result, both cues decrease pERK1/2 levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), an upstream activator of the TOR signalling pathway, which is known to regulate axonal protein synthesis (Campbell and Holt, 2003).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Netrin-1 can induce the rapid selective translation of specific mRNAs despite decreasing global translation.
source: Despite the decrease in global axonal translation, previous work has revealed that Netrin-1 can induce the rapid selective translation of specific mRNAs (Cagnetta et al., 2018; Shigeoka et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: DCC associates with mRNAs encoding β-catenin (ctnnb1) and hnRNPH1 (hnrnph1) significantly more than Nrp1 in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: The IP-RNA-seq data in human SH-SY5Y cells had revealed that DCC associates with mRNAs encoding β-catenin (ctnnb1) and hnRNPH1 (hnrnph1) significantly more than with Nrp1.
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data from SH-SY5Y cells.

claim: ctnnb1 and hnrnph1 mRNAs have been detected in Xenopus retinal axons.
source: Interestingly, ctnnb1 and hnrnph1 mRNAs have been detected in Xenopus retinal axons (Shigeoka et al., 2019) and are selectively synthesised in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A (Cagnetta et al., 2018), indicating that receptor-specific mRNAs can underlie the cue-induced selective translation.
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: ctnnb1 and hnrnph1 mRNAs are selectively synthesised in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A.
source: Interestingly, ctnnb1 and hnrnph1 mRNAs have been detected in Xenopus retinal axons (Shigeoka et al., 2019) and are selectively synthesised in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A (Cagnetta et al., 2018), indicating that receptor-specific mRNAs can underlie the cue-induced selective translation.
evidence: Supported by previous study cited.

claim: Receptor-specific mRNAs can underlie the cue-induced selective translation.
source: Interestingly, ctnnb1 and hnrnph1 mRNAs have been detected in Xenopus retinal axons (Shigeoka et al., 2019) and are selectively synthesised in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A (Cagnetta et al., 2018), indicating that receptor-specific mRNAs can underlie the cue-induced selective translation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mRNAs associated with specific receptors are selectively translated in response to cognate ligands.

claim: ctnnb1 and hnrnph1 mRNAs associate with DCC in Xenopus brain and eyes.
source: To further test this, we examined whether these mRNAs associate with DCC also in Xenopus brain and eyes by carrying out IP followed by qPCR. The results showed significant enrichment of ctnnb1 and hnrnph1 mRNAs in DCC pulldown compared to an IgG pulldown, thus confirming their association with DCC (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Both β-catenin and hnRNPH1 protein levels increase in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A.
source: Finally, quantification of immunofluorescence confirmed that both β-catenin and hnRNPH1 protein levels increase in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A (Figure 4E–H), in line with previous axonal translation findings (Cagnetta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4E–H.

claim: RPS14/uS11 mRNA is present in Xenopus retinal axons.
source: Similar to β-catenin and hnRNPH1, RPS14/uS11 mRNA is present in Xenopus retinal axons (Shigeoka et al., 2019) and is up-regulated in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A (Cagnetta et al., 2018), as confirmed by quantification of immunofluorescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by previous study cited and immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RPS14/uS11 is up-regulated in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A.
source: Similar to β-catenin and hnRNPH1, RPS14/uS11 mRNA is present in Xenopus retinal axons (Shigeoka et al., 2019) and is up-regulated in response to 5 min Netrin-1 stimulation, but not Sema3A (Cagnetta et al., 2018), as confirmed by quantification of immunofluorescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by previous study cited and immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: rps14 mRNA associates with DCC in Xenopus brain and eyes.
source: To address this question, we carried out IP followed by qPCR in Xenopus brain and eyes, which confirmed rps14 association to DCC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Netrin-1, but not Sema3A, induces the translation of mRNAs bound to DCC.
source: Our findings that Netrin-1, but not Sema3A, induces the translation of mRNAs bound to DCC point towards a model where receptor-specific mRNA interactomes act as a hub for rapid cue-specific selective translation.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing DCC-associated mRNAs are translated in response to Netrin-1 but not Sema3A.

claim: Receptor-specific mRNA interactomes act as a hub for rapid cue-specific selective translation.
source: Our findings that Netrin-1, but not Sema3A, induces the translation of mRNAs bound to DCC point towards a model where receptor-specific mRNA interactomes act as a hub for rapid cue-specific selective translation.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing receptor-specific mRNA associations and cue-specific translation.

claim: EphrinA1 stimulation alone does not affect β-catenin and RPS14/uS11 protein levels.
source: Quantification of immunofluorescence showed that EphrinA1 stimulation alone does not affect β-catenin and RPS14/uS11 protein levels (Figure 4E–H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and decreases hnRNPH1 protein level in axonal growth cones (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4E–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: EphrinA1 stimulation alone decreases hnRNPH1 protein level in axonal growth cones.
source: Quantification of immunofluorescence showed that EphrinA1 stimulation alone does not affect β-catenin and RPS14/uS11 protein levels (Figure 4E–H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and decreases hnRNPH1 protein level in axonal growth cones (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4G–H.

claim: Co-stimulation with Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 blocks the Netrin-1-induced increase of β-catenin, hnRNPH1, and RPS14/uS11 proteins.
source: Co-stimulation with Netrin-1 and EphrinA1 blocks the Netrin-1-induced increase of all three proteins (Figure 4E–H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 4E–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Integration of the EphrinA1 and Netrin-1 signals inhibits the Netrin-1-induced selective translation, possibly by inhibiting DCC-ribosome dissociation.
source: Together, the results show that integration of the EphrinA1 and Netrin-1 signals inhibits the Netrin-1-induced selective translation, possibly by inhibiting DCC-ribosome dissociation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EphrinA1 blocks both DCC-ribosome dissociation and Netrin-1-induced selective translation.

claim: Receptor-ribosome coupling is a common mechanism across different receptors and cell types.
source: Together, this study provides evidence that receptor-ribosome coupling is a common mechanism across different receptors and cell types, and suggests that receptor-specific interactomes act as a hub to regulate the localized and selective cue-induced mRNA translation.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing multiple receptors in different systems exhibit receptor-ribosome coupling.

claim: Receptor-specific interactomes act as a hub to regulate the localized and selective cue-induced mRNA translation.
source: Together, this study provides evidence that receptor-ribosome coupling is a common mechanism across different receptors and cell types, and suggests that receptor-specific interactomes act as a hub to regulate the localized and selective cue-induced mRNA translation.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing receptor-specific RBPs, mRNAs, and cue-induced selective translation.

claim: Receptor-ribosome coupled mechanism allows extrinsic cues to cause rapid and selective changes in the local proteome.
source: We provide evidence for a receptor-ribosome coupled mechanism by which extrinsic cues cause rapid and selective changes in the local proteome.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing receptor-ribosome coupling, cue-induced dissociation, and selective translation.

claim: Multiple guidance cue receptors interact with ribosomes.
source: In support of this model, we show that multiple guidance cue receptors interact with ribosomes, that the interaction between receptors and ribosomes depends on mRNA and rapidly decreases within 2 min of cue stimulation.
evidence: Supported by the collective data showing DCC, Nrp1, and Robo2 interact with ribosomes.

claim: The interaction between receptors and ribosomes depends on mRNA.
source: In support of this model, we show that multiple guidance cue receptors interact with ribosomes, that the interaction between receptors and ribosomes depends on mRNA and rapidly decreases within 2 min of cue stimulation.
evidence: Supported by the RNase treatment experiments showing decreased receptor-ribosome association.

claim: The interaction between receptors and ribosomes rapidly decreases within 2 min of cue stimulation.
source: In support of this model, we show that multiple guidance cue receptors interact with ribosomes, that the interaction between receptors and ribosomes depends on mRNA and rapidly decreases within 2 min of cue stimulation.
evidence: Supported by the PLA experiments showing decreased signal after 2 min cue stimulation.

claim: Receptors bind to distinct subsets of RBPs and mRNAs.
source: Moreover, we find that receptors bind to distinct subsets of RBPs and mRNAs, and that cue stimulation induces the selective axonal translation of several receptor-specific mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by the mass spectrometry and RNA-sequencing data showing receptor-specific associations.

claim: Cue stimulation induces the selective axonal translation of several receptor-specific mRNAs.
source: Moreover, we find that receptors bind to distinct subsets of RBPs and mRNAs, and that cue stimulation induces the selective axonal translation of several receptor-specific mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence data showing cue-specific translation of receptor-associated mRNAs.

claim: The integration of multiple cues can alter receptor-ribosome dissociation and selective translation.
source: Finally, we show that the integration of multiple cues can alter receptor-ribosome dissociation and selective translation.
evidence: Supported by the experiments showing EphrinA1 blocks Netrin-1-induced effects.

claim: Whether or not a particular receptor shows receptor-ribosome coupling is related to whether or not the receptors regulate local translation upon ligand binding.
source: Based on the candidate receptors tested here, we suggest that whether or not a particular receptor shows receptor-ribosome coupling is related to whether or not the receptors regulate local translation upon ligand binding.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that DCC, Nrp1, and Robo2 (which regulate local translation) interact with ribosomes, while EphB2 (which does not) does not.

claim: A chemokine receptor, CXCR4, associates with eukaryotic initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), which decreases upon ligand binding in a pre-B cell line.
source: Interestingly, a previous study has reported the association of a chemokine receptor, CXCR4, with eukaryotic initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), which decreases upon ligand binding in a pre-B cell line (Palmesino et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by previous study cited.

claim: Several adrenergic receptor subtypes have been reported to associate with eIF2B at the plasma membrane.
source: In addition, several adrenergic receptor subtypes have been reported to associate with eIF2B at the plasma membrane (Klein et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by previous study cited.

claim: Coupling of translational machinery with receptors may extend to other cell types and is a widespread mechanism to rapidly transduce local translation downstream of extracellular signals.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that coupling of translational machinery with receptors extends to other cell types and is a widespread mechanism to rapidly transduce local translation downstream of extracellular signals.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation of receptor-translation machinery coupling in different systems.

claim: The RBP zipcode binding protein 1 (ZBP1) can be phosphorylated upon cue stimulation, thereby regulating local translation in axons by possibly releasing the bound mRNAs.
source: Previous studies have shown that the RBP zipcode binding protein 1 (ZBP1) can be phosphorylated upon cue stimulation, thereby regulating local translation in axons by possibly releasing the bound mRNAs (Hüttelmaier et al., 2005; Sasaki et al., 2010; Lepelletier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: DCC and Nrp1 each differentially bind to RBPs and mRNAs, thus providing a way to rapidly achieve cue-induced selective translation.
source: DCC and Nrp1 each differentially bind to RBPs and mRNAs, thus providing a way to rapidly achieve cue-induced selective translation.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing receptor-specific RBP and mRNA associations.

claim: hnRNPA2B1 has been reported to control the translation of β-catenin.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the enrichment of the RBP hnRNPA2B1 and ctnnb1 mRNA (encoding β-catenin) specifically in DCC but not Nrp1 pulldown, as hnRNPA2B1 has been reported to control the translation of β-catenin (Stockley et al., 2014), which is selectively translated in response to Netrin-1, but not Sema3A in retinal axons (Cagnetta et al., 2018), in accord with the data reported here.
evidence: Supported by previous study cited.

claim: β-catenin is selectively translated in response to Netrin-1, but not Sema3A in retinal axons.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the enrichment of the RBP hnRNPA2B1 and ctnnb1 mRNA (encoding β-catenin) specifically in DCC but not Nrp1 pulldown, as hnRNPA2B1 has been reported to control the translation of β-catenin (Stockley et al., 2014), which is selectively translated in response to Netrin-1, but not Sema3A in retinal axons (Cagnetta et al., 2018), in accord with the data reported here.
evidence: Supported by previous study cited and data in this manuscript.

claim: RNA-seq analysis reveals a receptor-specific enrichment of 100–400 mRNAs suggesting that a large number of mRNAs may be regulated by specific receptors and their ligands.
source: Our RNA-seq analysis reveals a receptor-specific enrichment of 100–400 mRNAs suggesting that a large number of mRNAs may be regulated by specific receptors and their ligands (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The translation of more than 100 mRNAs is regulated within 5 min in response to Netrin-1 and Sema3A in Xenopus retinal axons.
source: This idea is consistent with our previous proteomics study in Xenopus retinal axons showing that the translation of more than 100 mRNAs is regulated within 5 min in response to Netrin-1 and Sema3A (Cagnetta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by previous proteomics study cited.

claim: Not all detected mRNAs interact with DCC and Nrp1 at the plasma membrane as a portion of these mRNAs could also be associated with receptors on endocytic vesicles.
source: In addition, it is possible that not all detected mRNAs interact with DCC and Nrp1 at the plasma membrane as a portion of these mRNAs could also be associated with receptors on endocytic vesicles that are known to contain DCC and Nrp1.
evidence: Speculated based on knowledge of receptor endocytosis.

claim: Different subsets of mRNAs interact via specific RBPs with either DCC or Nrp1, and are released, together with ribosomes, upon specific cue stimulation and thus become available for subsequent translation.
source: Our results point to a model in which different subsets of mRNAs interact via specific RBPs with either DCC or Nrp1, and are released, together with ribosomes, upon specific cue stimulation and thus become available for subsequent translation (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from the collective data and presented as a model in Figure 5.

claim: eIF3d, an initiation factor previously shown to regulate specialized translation initiation, is significantly enriched specifically after Nrp1 IP, but not DCC IP.
source: For example, eIF3d, an initiation factor previously shown to regulate specialized translation initiation, is significantly enriched specifically after Nrp1 IP, but not DCC IP, thus raising the interesting possibility that differential binding to initiation factors may contribute to cue-induced selective translation (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data and previous study cited.

claim: Differential binding to initiation factors may contribute to cue-induced selective translation.
source: For example, eIF3d, an initiation factor previously shown to regulate specialized translation initiation, is significantly enriched specifically after Nrp1 IP, but not DCC IP, thus raising the interesting possibility that differential binding to initiation factors may contribute to cue-induced selective translation (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculated based on the observation of differential eIF3d binding.

claim: An untranslated mRNA can associate with and regulate the signalling of the TrkA receptor in axons via its axon-enriched long 3'UTR.
source: Intriguingly, a recent study revealed that an untranslated mRNA can associate with and regulate the signalling of the TrkA receptor in axons via its axon-enriched long 3'UTR (Crerar et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by previous study cited.

claim: During axon guidance and branching, axons can encounter a combination of extracellular signals and the integration of multiple cues results in different outcomes than those of each single cue.
source: During axon guidance and branching, axons can encounter a combination of extracellular signals and ample evidence shows that the integration of multiple cues results in different outcomes than those of each single cue (Dudanova and Klein, 2013; Morales and Kania, 2017).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: EphrinA1 blocks the Netrin-1-induced ribosome dissociation from DCC, but not the Sema3A-induced ribosome dissociation from Nrp1.
source: Here, we tested the effect of cue integration on receptor-ribosome coupling and found that EphrinA1 blocks the Netrin-1-induced ribosome dissociation from DCC, but not the Sema3A-induced ribosome dissociation from Nrp1.
evidence: Supported by the PLA experiments with co-stimulation.

claim: EphrinA1 blocks the Netrin-1-induced selective increase in translation of several mRNAs.
source: In addition, EphrinA1 blocks the Netrin-1-induced selective increase in translation of several mRNAs.
evidence: Supported by the immunofluorescence quantification experiments with co-stimulation.

claim: Upon co-stimulation of EphrinA1 and Netrin-1, the DCC and Eph receptors may form a complex, thereby altering the receptor structure and association to ribosomes.
source: One possibility is that, upon co-stimulation of EphrinA1 and Netrin-1, the DCC and Eph receptors may form a complex, thereby altering the receptor structure and association to ribosomes, which could be consistent with a previous study revealing a ligand-dependent interaction between the receptors Unc5 and EphB2 (Poliak et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculated based on the observation of blocked ribosome dissociation and previous study showing receptor-receptor interactions.

claim: Coupling of the translational machinery to guidance cue receptors at the plasma membrane of growth cones is a mechanism to rapidly and selectively control the cue-induced regulation of the local proteome.
source: In conclusion, our findings show that coupling of the translational machinery to guidance cue receptors at the plasma membrane of growth cones is a mechanism to rapidly and selectively control the cue-induced regulation of the local proteome and suggest that this may be a general principle that applies to membrane receptors more broadly.
evidence: Inferred from the collective data showing receptor-ribosome coupling and cue-induced selective translation.

claim: Receptor-ribosome coupling may be a general principle that applies to membrane receptors more broadly.
source: In conclusion, our findings show that coupling of the translational machinery to guidance cue receptors at the plasma membrane of growth cones is a mechanism to rapidly and selectively control the cue-induced regulation of the local proteome and suggest that this may be a general principle that applies to membrane receptors more broadly.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation of receptor-ribosome coupling in multiple receptors and cell types.
